principles.claim: The GPU barely waits on the host, even at batch 1.
principles.evidence: No cell is under 90% busy beyond its noise; the least busy is 97% (TensorRT-LLM, 0.6B, batch 1).

principles.claim: Most of a 0.6B step is spent above the bandwidth floor, the largest part of it kernel excess; most of a 32B step is the floor.
principles.evidence: At batch 1 the floor is 23%–28% of a 0.6B step and 86%–88% of a 32B step. Above the floor, kernel excess is the largest part for every engine at 0.6B.

principles.claim: Engines differ most on small models.
principles.evidence: At the engine API (batch 1–16), the slowest step is up to 33% longer than the fastest at 0.6B, and 4.7% longer at 32B. vLLM is the fastest beyond noise in 15 of 50 cells compared; in 30 the fastest is within noise of another engine. Among the servers, TensorRT-LLM is up to 29% longer than the fastest.

principles.claim: Of the mitigations, CUDA graphs matter most.
principles.evidence: CUDA graphs off, the step is up to 8.5x as long (SGLang, 0.6B, batch 1); then async scheduling off, up to 1.6x as long (vLLM); overlap scheduler off, up to 1.5x as long (TensorRT-LLM). Within noise everywhere: model Runner V2 off.

principles.claim: The server stack costs nothing beyond noise over the engine API.
principles.evidence: Within noise in all 33 cells measured at both (0.6B–14B, batch 1–64); the most it could hide is 4.9% for vLLM, 1.0% for SGLang, 17% for TensorRT-LLM; the largest difference is 0.7% (± 5.3%, one SD; TensorRT-LLM, 0.6B, batch 1). HTTP, streaming, detokenising and the server's own scheduling together. Not compared: all 3 server cells rejected, TensorRT-LLM at 32–64 streams on 0.6B–4B (sequences fell behind the batch: a frontend that could not keep its streams even on this host).
